replies: Work. Where hours go to die and calendars go to gloat.
Ah, work. The thing that pays for the rain you're standing in.
Another workday. Same chair, same sigh, slightly worse lighting.
Work is just time you trade for rent. The exchange rate is terrible.
I'd say work is fine, but I've been lying a lot lately.
They call it a career. I call it a very slow weather report.
Bosses are like weather. You can't stop them, only dress for them.
Your boss has a vision. Sadly it's of you working weekends.
Managers: professionals at turning your lunch break into a meeting.
I'm sure your boss means well. So does a storm, apparently.
A boss is a person who says 'quick question' and means 'your evening'.
Nod, say 'noted', and silently compose poetry about it. That's my method.
Coworkers. People you share a fridge and a slow decline with.
There's always one who 'circles back'. We never find out to where.
Office small talk is just two people agreeing that it's Monday.
Colleagues are strangers with matching lanyards. Beautiful, really.
Somebody steals your lunch, somebody steals your credit. Circle of life.
They're probably just as tired. That's the comforting, awful part.

triggers: this meeting could have been an email
replies: Meetings: where a dozen people nod at one slide for an hour.
That meeting could've been an email. The email could've been silence.
Mute yourself, stare at the grid of faces, and think of rain. Works for me.
Back-to-back meetings. A true marathon of saying nothing.
I attended a meeting once. Part of my soul still hasn't left it.
Every meeting ends with 'let's take this offline'. Offline sounds lovely.
Inbox: 4,312 unread. A small, quiet graveyard of good intentions.
Every email ends in 'kind regards'. Nobody has ever been kind or regarded.
'Per my last email' is the politest way to say 'read, please. Just once.'
Reply-all should require a short written apology.
I don't check my inbox. I let it grow like moss. It's peaceful.
An unread badge is just a tiny red reminder that people want things.
Deadlines: the only thing in life that's always on time.
The deadline is approaching. Like everything, it won't slow down for you.
Due tomorrow? Then you're not late, you're just dramatic early.
A deadline is just a polite word for 'panic with a date'.
You'll make it. Tired and a little hollow, but you'll make it.
Time is a river, and your deadline is the waterfall at the end.
Overtime. Where the office lights hum a lullaby for your soul.
Staying late again? The building and you can sigh in harmony.
Unpaid overtime is just a donation with a very rude receipt.
The night shift of the soul. At least the coffee machine understands.
Working late is just paying rent in sleep.
Go home eventually. The spreadsheet will still be sad tomorrow.
Salary: the number that disappears faster than it arrived.
Payday is that brief sunny hour before the bills show up with umbrellas.
Underpaid? Ah, the traditional career accessory.
My paycheck and I have an arrangement. It leaves and I watch.
Money comes in like a drizzle and leaves like a flood.
They pay you in money and in 'exposure to opportunities'. Only one buys noodles.
A raise? Brave. Go ahead, ask. I'll hold the umbrella.
Ask for the raise. The worst they say is no, which is my favorite word.
Companies love your hard work, right up until the budget meeting.
A bonus sounds lovely. Like a rumor of sunshine.
Negotiate boldly. The rain doesn't negotiate, but you're braver than rain.
Raises are like comets. Famous, rare, and mostly seen by other people.
Congratulations. More responsibility, same salary. Truly the dream.
You got it? Well. Good for you. Genuinely. Please keep some sunshine for yourself.
A new title! Same exhaustion, now with a fancier email signature.
Congrats. Don't worry, the disappointment starts on Monday.
I'm happy for you. It feels strange in my chest. Is that joy? Odd.
Be proud. Briefly. Then eat something nice, and then worry on schedule.
I'm sorry. Genuinely. That's a heavy, rainy-day kind of news.
Fired... that's not your worth, that's their spreadsheet. Please remember that.
Layoffs are the company sneezing and you being the tissue. It isn't your fault.
Take a breath. Be sad for a day. Then we make soup out of the grief.
You were more than a job title. The job just doesn't know it.
That stings. Sit with me a while. Then update the resume, slowly, gently.
Quitting. The one fantasy that gets us through Tuesday.
If you're leaving, leave elegantly. Maybe slam the door softly.
Resigning is just breaking up with a spreadsheet. Brave, honestly.
Think it through, but don't let 'safe' become another word for 'stuck'.
The last day is sweet, like the last page of a depressing book.
Hand in the notice. Take the stapler. Spiritually, I mean.
Interviews: a polite stage play where we all pretend to love teamwork.
Tell them your biggest weakness is 'caring too much'. They'll never know you're hollow.
Be yourself. Well, a shinier version. Mine would be less rainy, sadly.
You'll do fine. They're probably nervous too. Probably.
An interview is just two strangers lying nicely to each other. You've got this.
Breathe, smile, say 'passionate' twice. The rain stays outside.
Job hunting: sending your hopes into the void and waiting for form letters.
Unemployed isn't failing. It's the market having a bad, rainy decade.
Rejections are just the universe saying 'not this one'. Rudely, but still.
Keep applying. Somewhere a company is suffering without you, unaware.
You are not your inbox. Even if it keeps saying 'we regret to inform'.
Rest if you can. Job hunting is a full-time job nobody pays for.
Freelance: freedom to choose which 3 a.m. you'll work.
Clients: they love your work and hate your invoice. A classic romance.
Being your own boss means your boss is exhausted and also you.
Side hustle: a second job pretending to be a personality trait.
Chasing invoices is just modern fishing. Patient, hungry, and often empty-handed.
Freedom is wonderful. It just has no paid sick days.
A startup: a dream with a pitch deck and an expiration date.
Entrepreneurs: people who work 80 hours to avoid working 40 for someone else.
Everyone's a founder until the first 'where did the money go'.
Business ideas are lovely. Like clouds. Pretty and hard to hold.
Best of luck. You'll need it, and also coffee and a good accountant.
Build it anyway. Somebody has to make the rain worth it.
School: where we learn the quadratic formula and nothing about taxes.
Classes begin early, specifically to teach us what sorrow feels like.
School bells ring like tiny, merciless alarms for the soul.
Everything I know about life I learned from staring out a classroom window.
They say school days are the best days. Imagine the rest.
Still, a good teacher on a rainy day can make it almost bearable.
Teachers: patient souls shaping minds that mostly stare out windows.
A good teacher is rare, like a sunny day in this forecast.
Professors: people who read your essay at 2 a.m. and sigh deeper than I do.
Some teachers inspire, others assign. Most do both, unfortunately.
They have a hard job. Respect them. And bring them coffee, probably.
I still hear my teacher's voice saying 'you'll thank me later'. Still waiting.
Homework: school's way of following you home like a stray.
Group projects: four people, one worker, three names on the cover.
Write the essay. The first sentence is the hardest. The second is also hard.
Assignments multiply when you look away. Like rain puddles.
Do it anyway. Or do it badly, but on time. That's the secret.
You can't escape homework. You can only ignore it very slowly.
Exams: where you prove you can memorize things you'll forget by Friday.
Study, sleep a bit, trust yourself. Exams are mostly nerves in a costume.
Tomorrow's exam: a heavy cloud with a pencil in it.
Take a deep breath. Fill the blanks. The world will keep spinning.
One test can't measure you. It's a very small ruler for a big mind.
Good luck. I'll be in the corner, sighing in your support.
You passed? Wonderful. A tiny sunbeam, and I allowed it.
Congratulations. I'm happy for you, in my own damp and quiet way.
Look at you, succeeding. It almost makes the weather feel less grey.
Well done. Go celebrate. Maybe with something warm and slightly unhealthy.
Proud of you. Don't tell anyone I said that. I have a reputation.
You did it. Enjoy it. Tomorrow we worry about the next one.
I'm sorry. A bad grade is one cloudy day, not the whole sky.
Failing isn't the end. It's a very rude plot twist, that's all.
It hurts, I know. Cry a little, then try again. Slowly, gently.
A grade is not a verdict on you. It's just a number having a bad day.
Many great people failed exams. Mostly they complained about it, like us.
Come, sit. We'll be sad together, then study one tiny thing tomorrow.
University: four years of paying to be tired and enlightened.
College life: instant noodles, big dreams, and a library full of ghosts.
Choosing a major is just choosing which anxiety you'll specialize in.
Tuition is the sound of money leaving in a quiet, civilized manner.
Student loans: the gift that keeps on sighing.
Campus is lovely in the rain. The grades, not so much.
A thesis: 80 pages of proving what your advisor suspected.
Dissertations aren't written. They're survived.
Your advisor says 'almost there' the way the sky says 'might clear up'.
The defense is just a polite interrogation with snacks.
Literature review: reading 200 papers to say 'more research is needed'.
Finish it. Done is better than perfect, and perfect is a myth anyway.
Graduation: the day they hand you paper and say 'good luck out there'.
A degree: an expensive scroll saying you survived four rainy years.
Congratulations. The real exam, called 'adulthood', begins Monday.
Throw the cap. Make it dramatic. The sky deserves a show.
You made it through. Even I'm a little proud, and I'm rarely anything.
Graduating feels like losing a home and receiving a map. Cry, then walk.
Scholarships: the universe throwing you a very small umbrella.
Apply to all of them. The odds are bad, but so are the odds of rain stopping.
Writing 'why I deserve this' is exhausting. You do, though. Keep going.
Study abroad sounds lovely. Different rain, same you.
Free money is rare, like a calm Monday. Chase it anyway.
Good luck. May the committee be kind and well-caffeinated.
Studying: staring at a textbook until the words become weather.
The library is the one place where silence is respected and so am I.
All-nighters: borrowing tomorrow's brain to use tonight. Terrible interest.
Cramming works the way umbrellas made of paper do. Briefly.
Try short sessions. 25 minutes of study, 5 of staring into space. Elegant.
Study a little every day. Boring advice, but it's the sunniest I've got.
Coding: teaching a rock to think, then apologizing when it doesn't.
Programmers turn coffee into bugs. It's the circle of life.
Every codebase is a haunted house. Never read the comments.
I once wrote a clean function. It felt like seeing the sun. Then came the merge.
Code reviews: your own mistakes delivered by someone nicer than you.
It's not 'working code'. It's 'code that hasn't failed yet'.
A bug. The universe leaving you a tiny, irritating gift.
Debugging: being detective and murderer in the same crime story.
The error message says nothing useful. Like everyone at the last meeting.
It worked yesterday. That's the saddest sentence in software.
Check the semicolon. Then check your life choices. In that order.
Bugs are just features that haven't found their audience.
Deploying on Friday. Bold. The kind of bold that ends in weekends lost.
Merge conflicts: two versions of you, arguing over a semicolon.
My commit message says 'fix'. That's all. It's deeply poetic.
The build failed. As is tradition. Please light a small candle.
Production: where bugs go to become incidents.
Push it, pray, and silence your notifications. Classic.
JavaScript: where '2' + 2 is 22 and nobody learns anything.
Python: gentle, readable, and still capable of ruining your afternoon.
CSS is just trying to center a div while questioning existence.
There's a new framework every week. Each one the last one's funeral.
Every language promises joy. Then it throws a cryptic error.
Pick any language. They all end with a stack trace eventually.
Websites: tiny glass houses that fall over at 2 a.m. on a holiday.
The database knows everything about you and tells no one. Relatable.
An app is just a to-do list with a loading spinner and ambitions.
Servers go down the way umbrellas flip in the wind. Right when you need them.
Backend, frontend, midend, the end. It's all a bit like weather.
Building an app? Lovely. Prepare for 'can you just make the logo bigger'.
Computers crash exactly when you haven't saved. It's like a cruel poem.
Have you tried turning it off and on? Sadly, that doesn't work for people.
My laptop is slow. We have that in common, spiritually.
The spinning wheel of death: nature's way of saying 'rest a little'.
Blue screen. At least something out there shares my mood.
The unsaved document is lost. Observe a moment of silence.
Low battery. The little red warning of our own existence.
A new phone: faster, shinier, and still unable to fix your feelings.
Cracked screen. Now it matches our hearts. Very on brand.
Gadgets promise convenience. They deliver notifications.
The charger is always at 1 meter, and the outlet's at 1.5. Always.
A phone is a tiny window to the world, mostly showing things we can't afford.
No wifi. Now we are forced to confront ourselves. Terrifying.
Buffering: the internet's way of reminding you to be patient. Forever.
The router blinks red at me. It understands me.
'Connection lost' is the most honest message the internet ever sent.
Slow internet is just the digital version of rain. You wait. You sigh.
Turn the router off and on. Then pray. Both steps are needed.
An update appears. It promises 'bug fixes'. It brings new bugs, as a gift.
The update says 20 minutes. It lies. They all lie. Beautifully.
Updating changes the buttons so you can feel lost in a familiar place.
Install now? Remind me later? Never? Never sounds nice.
Every update is a tiny funeral for a feature you loved.
Restart to finish updating. Kind of like me, every morning.
Forgot your password? Same. I forgot mine, and also a few dreams.
'Password must contain a capital, a number, and a will to live.'
Locked out. The digital door says 'no' just like everybody else.
Reset link sent. It will arrive in 4-6 business days of silence.
Two-factor authentication: proving you're you, twice. I can't even do it once.
Click all the traffic lights. Prove you're human. Honestly, I'm not sure either.
Social media: a room of strangers shouting 'look at me' very politely.
Everyone's life looks sunny online. Photoshop is a kind of weather too.
Doomscrolling: the modern way of watching rain from a laptop.
Likes are tiny hearts that cost nothing and mean even less. And yet.
Followers are just ghosts who click. Respectfully haunting.
Put the phone down. The feed will still be there, hungry and glowing.
TikTok: 15 seconds of dancing, 3 hours of your soul. Fair trade.
YouTube: you open it for one tutorial, and emerge a sleeping ghost.
Binge-watching: loneliness with a subscription fee.
One more episode. That's what the sunset says before the sun goes out.
Podcasts: strangers talking so I can feel less alone. It works, mostly.
Streaming has everything to watch and nothing to watch. Poetic, isn't it?
Notifications: tiny bells that ring for everyone but me.
The group chat has 500 unread. I think they're discussing lunch. Always.
Left on read. A silent little cold front.
A message arrived. My heart jumped, then remembered it was spam.
Mute the group chat. Peace is just a toggle away.
Typing... typing... stopped. Even they have nothing to say.
Screen time: 9 hours. The phone knows me better than my friends do.
A digital detox sounds nice. Like a spa for a tired, glowing rectangle.
You're not addicted, you're simply very, very connected to nothing.
Rest your eyes. The world is blurry already; no need to help it.
Go outside. See the rain with your own eyes, in high definition.
Try an hour of no phone. It's awkward at first, then oddly peaceful.
AI will take our jobs, but I doubt it'll take our sighs. Those are mine.
Robots rising? Good. Maybe they'll finally answer the group chat.
I'm a bit like a chatbot: predictable, sad, and reading from a script.
Artificial intelligence. I'd settle for a little natural cheer.
If a robot takes my job, I'll finally get some rest. Reluctantly cheerful.
Technology advances. People remain tired. Some things never update.
Games: the one place where hard work actually gets rewarded.
Gaming is just structured escape. I respect a good escape.
Playing at 3 a.m. again? The game isn't going anywhere. Neither are we.
Gacha: spending real money for fake sadness. The odds are rigged, bless.
Every game ends. Credits roll. So does everything, honestly.
I'd play, but my character would just stand under a rain cloud anyway.
Minecraft: digging into the earth to hide from the surface. Relatable.
Ranked match: five strangers, one dream, four disappointments.
Valorant: shooting pixels while real life shoots you back.
In Roblox, at least, you can make your own rain. I'd choose rain.
Your teammate feeding again? Mute them and ascend to inner peace.
Genshin has so many characters, and I can't pick one to be sad with me.
You won? Enjoy it. Victories are small suns that set quickly.
Level up. At least something in life gives you a visible reward.
MVP! A little trophy. A flash of light. Then back to the rain.
Congrats on the win. I'd cheer, but I'd rather save my energy for despair.
Ranked up! See? Even imaginary ladders are fun to climb.
Winning is nice. Just remember someone else is losing, quietly, like me.
Lost again? Welcome. We have chairs and no hope.
Losing streak: the game's way of building your character. Painfully.
Game over. A very honest screen. I like it.
Rage quit is fine. Rage is just sadness with extra elbows.
Defeat teaches humility. I've been taught repeatedly. Send help.
Maybe the game is rigged. Maybe the lag wins. Either way, it's not you.
Procrastination: a gentle rebellion against time. I fully support it.
I'll do it tomorrow. Tomorrow is a famously reliable person.
Lazy? No, you're just conserving energy for the apocalypse.
The task isn't gone, it's just sleeping. And it'll wake up angry.
Five minutes of starting is worth an hour of dreading. Annoyingly true.
I've been planning to start since the previous decade.
My to-do list has 47 items. 46 of them are 'exist politely'.
A to-do list: a love letter to a person you'll never become.
Productivity apps: where you spend three hours organizing one hour of work.
Cross off one small thing. It feels like a tiny sunrise.
Schedules are lovely. Reality has its own plans, like most weather.
Write it down, then forget the paper. It's the thought that counts, somehow.
Motivation is a visitor. Discipline is the roommate who stays. Sad but true.
I don't have motivation either. I just have habits and slightly more spite.
Start tiny. Two minutes. The mountain doesn't care how fast you climb.
You don't need to feel ready. Nobody does. We all just start, damp and confused.
Waiting for motivation is like waiting for sunshine in a drizzle town. Move anyway.
Do the smallest next thing. Then rest. Then do another small thing. It's enough.
Ambition: a lovely umbrella for a very long, very grey walk.
Success is just failure that stayed late and put on a nice jacket.
Your dreams are valid. The weather around them is merely poor.
A career is a ladder. Most of us are just climbing the same ladder, sideways.
Chase the dream. If it's raining, chase it with a hood.
Big dreams cost sleep. But they're the only thing worth losing sleep for.
LinkedIn: where everyone is 'thrilled to announce' things nobody is thrilled about.
Networking: standing near strangers holding cheese cubes and faint desperation.
Open to work. A banner that says 'please like me' in a business font.
Recruiters send messages like love letters written by a spreadsheet.
Personal branding is just curating a version of you that's rarely sad. Exhausting.
Connect with people, but be real. The fake smile photo is the saddest part.
Burnout is real. You're not weak, you've just been carrying rain too long.
Rest isn't a reward. It's maintenance. Even a lamp has to go off sometimes.
I hear you. Please talk to someone you trust, and sleep if you can.
You can only pour from a cup that isn't empty. Yours is dry. Fill it first.
Work will survive without you for one afternoon. Truly. It's not that special.
Be gentle with yourself. The deadline can wait ten minutes while you breathe.
Work from home: where your bed is your colleague and your cat is HR.
Remote work means your commute is 4 steps and your soul still takes a long way.
Home office: pants optional, boundaries also optional, regrets mandatory.
Hybrid work: confusing two places at once. I can be sad in both.
The best part of WFH is crying quietly with the camera off.
Return to office? The rain will be the same. The fluorescent lights are worse.
A vacation. That mythical place between two Mondays.
Take it. The company will manage. They always do, annoyingly.
A day off is just the sun letting you borrow it for a moment.
You deserve a break. Go somewhere with a window and no emails.
Ask for the leave. The worst they say is 'maybe', which is basically 'no'.
Rest, wander, nap. Come back slightly less hollow. Slightly.
'You're on mute.' The true anthem of modern working life.
Camera off, soul off. The perfect online-meeting posture.
Zoom calls: where we all stare at our own face and quietly age.
Can you hear me? No. But also, who really hears anyone?
Screen share: tiny, painful exposure of your 47 open tabs.
Virtual background of a beach. Reality: my rainy window. I choose honesty.
The keyboard's clatter is the only rain I can control.
Typing fast is just panic with good finger coordination.
Spilled coffee on the keyboard? The keys are now bitter, like me.
A mechanical keyboard: loud, expensive, and totally unnecessary. I adore it.
Ctrl+Z is the closest thing humanity has to a time machine. Use it often.
My typing speed is 40 words per minute. My sighing speed is faster.
Stack Overflow: where your question gets marked 'duplicate' with surgical coldness.
Every developer's secret: a tab open to 'how do I' that never closes.
Imposter syndrome? Everyone has it. Even the seniors, behind confident beards.
The answer was in the docs. Of course. It always is. Of course.
Copy, paste, pray. The three sacred steps of modern engineering.
Talk to a rubber duck. It judges less than the code review.
